video.title: How Scap Retraction Powers the One-Handed Backhand

classification.reason: The coach teaches the mechanics, pull slot position, wrist control, and grip alignment needed to execute a fault-tolerant one-handed backhand powered by scapular retraction.

problem.title_as_question: How do you properly power and control the one-handed backhand using scapular retraction?
problem.definition: Players often try to pull late or with weak arm muscles, let their wrist naively break across contact, or hold a slanted grip, which causes inconsistent string angles and a lack of drive.

symptoms.description: The player catches the ball too close to the stomach or behind the body, unable to exert upper-back pulling strength.
The swing pulls sideways across the body instead of driving straight through back-to-front toward the target.
Over-rotating the torso on a purely one-handed swing resulting in shanking the ball.
The wrist breaks open up to 100 degrees through the hitting zone, causing wild string angle changes.

causes.statement: The pull is initiated from the wrong spatial slot (too late or close to the stomach), robbing upper back leverage.
The player attempts to generate force using small, weak arm muscles like the triceps or deltoid rather than upper back scapular retraction.
Pulling exclusively with one hand rather than supporting the forward drive with a two-handed motion.
Allowing the wrist to naively and freely break through contact instead of maintaining forearm tension.
Holding the grip with the knuckles slanted relative to the handle rather than maintaining a 90-degree orthogonal angle.

angles.summary: Scapular retraction pulls the rhomboids and traps together to drive the racket forward from the proper pull slot.

On the forehand wrist relaxation naturally maintains string stability until after contact, whereas naively relaxing on the one-handed backhand causes the wrist to break prematurely right through the contact zone.
A 90-degree orthogonal angle between the forearm and handle allows forearm rotation without disrupting string angle, unlike a slanted grip.

solutions.summary: Test pull slot force generation against a wall to locate the contact zone where upper back muscles can exert maximum pulling strength.
solutions.external_goal: Push or pull against a wall to test whether force is produced from the upper back.

solutions.summary: Keep both hands driving forward into the pull slot before splitting around contact to prevent over-rotation.

Start by preparing with the racket head down and keeping a rigid wrist angle through contact like a block shot, then progressively loosen preparation and add dynamic racket head rotation as control develops.
solutions.external_goal: Maintain static racket head angle through contact before advancing to a looser whip.

solutions.summary: Align the knuckles parallel along the handle to enforce a 90-degree orthogonal angle between forearm and racket.
solutions.external_goal: Keep the handle perpendicular to the forearm with knuckles parallel to the racket handle.
